Kohl is a dark substance — almost always black or very dark grey — that people apply around their eyes as a cosmetic. Think of it as the ancient world's eye makeup: part eyeliner, part eye shadow, all in one.

Traditional kohl is an extremely fine, soft powder or paste made from natural minerals ground down until they're almost silky smooth. The most common ingredient historically was galena, a naturally occurring mineral that is essentially a dark, metallic grey-black material. Other versions were made from antimony sulfide (another dark mineral), charcoal, soot from oil lamps, or burnt almonds — sometimes blended with oils or fats to make a paste.

It is stored in a small container called a kohl pot or kohl jar, which is often beautifully decorated. To apply it, you dip a thin stick (made from wood, ivory, bone, or metal) into the pot and carefully draw it along the inner rim of the eyelid, along the upper lash line, or beneath the eye. The result is a bold, dark, slightly smoky outline that makes the eyes look dramatically defined.
Where it comes from and who uses it

Kohl is not a niche or exotic product — it has one of the longest and most widespread histories of any cosmetic in human existence.

Ancient Egypt is probably the most famous example. In paintings and carvings of ancient Egyptians, you always notice that thick, dramatic dark line around their eyes. That is kohl — and importantly, both men and women wore it. Pharaohs, priests, commoners — everyone used it.

Beyond Egypt, kohl has been central to beauty culture across the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia for thousands of years. In the Arab world, it is known as kuhl (the word "kohl" in English actually comes from Arabic). In India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, a near-identical substance is called kajal or surma, and it is deeply woven into everyday life — not just as beauty product, but as part of cultural rituals, including putting it on newborn babies' eyes.

The reasons are layered and fascinating:

For beauty: The most obvious reason. Kohl makes eyes look larger, more intense, more expressive, and more striking. The smoky dark outline creates a powerful visual contrast, especially on lighter-coloured eyes, but equally dramatic on dark eyes.

For sun protection: In the scorching, sun-drenched climates of North Africa and the Middle East, the dark pigment applied around the eyes served a practical purpose — reducing the glare from the sun, much like how modern athletes put black grease beneath their eyes before games.

For perceived medicinal protection: People historically believed kohl could shield eyes from infections, dust, and disease. Interestingly, some researchers have suggested that certain ancient formulations may have had mild antibacterial properties, though this is still debated.

For spiritual and cultural protection: In many cultures, kohl is believed to ward off the "evil eye" — the idea that an envious or malicious gaze from another person can cause harm. Applying kohl, especially on children, was seen as a form of spiritual shielding.

Today, you will encounter the word "kohl" in two contexts:

1. Traditional kohl — still used in parts of the Middle East, South Asia, and North Africa in its original mineral-powder form. Health authorities now caution against lead-based versions (more on that below), but non-lead alternatives made from antimony or plant-based ingredients are still widely used.

2. Modern cosmetic products labelled "kohl" — Walk into any beauty shop and you'll see "kohl pencil" or "kohl eyeliner" on the shelves. These products are designed to replicate the dark, smoky, smudged look of traditional kohl, but they are made from modern synthetic and safer ingredients. They are not the same material as traditional kohl — they just borrow the name and the aesthetic.

Traditional kohl made from lead-based minerals is now known to be dangerous. Lead is a toxic substance that can be absorbed through the sensitive skin around the eyes, and it poses a serious health risk — especially to children. Many countries now ban or strictly regulate the import and sale of traditional lead-based kohl. If you ever see traditional kohl being sold, it's worth checking what it's made from. Modern products labelled "kohl" in mainstream shops are safe because they use regulated cosmetic ingredients.

Kohl is a finely powdered or pasted dark mineral cosmetic, applied around the eyes using a stick. It has been used for thousands of years across ancient Egypt, the Arab world, and South Asia — by men and women alike — for beauty, sun protection, and cultural or spiritual reasons. Today, the word also refers broadly to a style of dark, smoky eye cosmetic in mainstream beauty products. It sits at a rare intersection of art, culture, history, and daily life — a word that carries the weight of entire civilisations in it.
